intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that retinitis pigmentosa-7 (RP7) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the peripherin/RDS gene (PRPH2) on chromosome 6p. A digenic form of RP7 is caused by double heterozygous mutations in the PRPH2 and ROM1 genes. Homozygous mutation in PRPH2 has also been reported in patients with an early-onset retinal dystrophy with Leber congenital amaurosis/juvenile RP phenotypes.

checks.evidence_quote: Our results indicate that some cases of autosomal dominant retinitis pigmentosa are due to mutations at the RDS locus.
checks.explanation: The abstract links RDS mutations to autosomal dominant RP. It does not say the mutations are heterozygous or use the RP7 designation; those details may be in the full text, but only the abstract was supplied.

checks.explanation: RDS is listed among the chromosome 6p markers typed, and the gene is localized to 6p.

checks.evidence_quote: Three families were identified with mutations in the unlinked photoreceptor-specific genes ROM1 and peripherin/RDS, in which only double heterozygotes develop retinitis pigmentosa (RP).
checks.explanation: The abstract describes digenic RP in double heterozygotes for peripherin/RDS (PRPH2) and ROM1 mutations. Calling it 'RP7' is the OMIM entry's own label; the paper does not use that term.

checks.evidence_quote: To our knowledge, our study reported for the first time that homozygous mutations in PRPH2 cause EORD with LCA/juvenile RP phenotypes.

paragraphs.text: Retinitis pigmentosa-7 is a form of retinitis pigmentosa, a group of retinopathies characterized by photoreceptor degeneration, caused by mutation in the gene encoding peripherin/RDS, a photoreceptor-specific glycoprotein. It is usually inherited in an autosomal dominant manner, but a digenic form requiring heterozygous mutations in both PRPH2 and ROM1 has been described (Kajiwara et al., 1994). PRPH2 mutations produce highly variable phenotypes, and retinitis pigmentosa, pattern macular dystrophy, and fundus flavimaculatus can occur within a single family (Weleber et al., 1993; Manes et al., 2015).

checks.explanation: The abstract describes RP as a hereditary retinal degeneration characterized by photoreceptor degeneration.

checks.explanation: The abstract describes peripherin as a photoreceptor-specific glycoprotein and concludes that mutant peripherin causes the 6p-linked adRP. The name 'RP7' is standard nomenclature for this form.

paragraphs.text: Weleber et al. (1993) reported 3 separate phenotypes within a single family carrying a 3-bp deletion in the peripherin/RDS gene. The mother presented at age 63 years with a profoundly abnormal electroretinogram (ERG) and adult-onset retinitis pigmentosa that progressed dramatically over 12 years, with marked loss of peripheral visual field. One daughter developed pattern macular dystrophy at age 31 years; at age 44 years her ERG was moderately abnormal but her clinical disease was limited to the macula. Another daughter presented at age 42 years with macular degeneration and over 10 years developed the clinical picture of fundus flavimaculatus, with preserved peripheral visual field and a moderately abnormal ERG. The son had onset of macular degeneration at age 44 years, with pericentral scotomas, a markedly abnormal ERG, and punctate pigment epithelial transmission defects on fluorescein angiography.

paragraphs.text: Wang et al. (2013) described 3 patients homozygous for PRPH2 mutations who had Leber congenital amaurosis (LCA) or juvenile RP phenotypes, including visual impairment within the first year of life, nystagmus in the 2 LCA patients, nondetectable or reduced ERGs, and a very similar form of maculopathy. Fundus findings included multilobulated central atrophic maculopathy, vessel narrowing, pigment deposits, choroidal sclerosis, and optic disc pallor. Heterozygous family members were asymptomatic but showed maculopathy; for example, the 56-year-old father of 1 patient had macular pattern dystrophy with essentially normal visual acuity, and the asymptomatic 57-year-old mother of another patient had a florid butterfly-shaped macular pattern dystrophy and other retinal flecks.

paragraphs.text: By targeted next-generation sequencing of 163 retinal disease genes in 179 unrelated, prescreened patients with LCA or juvenile RP, Wang et al. (2013) identified homozygous PRPH2 missense mutations in 2 patients with LCA: C213R and L185P. Sequencing of PRPH2 in another 135 unsolved LCA or juvenile RP patients identified homozygosity for L185P in a third patient, who had juvenile RP. The mutations were confirmed by Sanger sequencing and segregation was examined; in 1 family the parents and son of the proband were heterozygous for C213R and an unaffected brother was homozygous wildtype, and in another family both parents of the proband were heterozygous for L185P. The authors noted that the L185P mutation, together with a null mutation in ROM1, had been reported to cause digenic RP.

agent.process_note: I read the index and all nine abstract-only or title-only files in full. Kikawa et al. (1994) has only a title. For Wang et al. (2013), the only full text, I searched for PRPH2, RDS, ROM1 and peripherin, then read the abstract, the introduction, the PRPH2 results and discussion, the figure legends and the mutation tables. The abstracts do not give the specific mutations reported by Kajiwara et al. (1991) or the PRPH2/ROM1 variants in Kajiwara et al. (1994), so I wrote no variant details for those papers. The Farrar et al. (1991) Nature abstract gives no codon for its 3-bp cysteine deletion, so I did not link it to the codon 118/119 deletion of Wells et al. (1993). No HGNC reference data were supplied, so the gene MIM number is left out and the chromosome location (6p) comes from the papers.
